Use case: stylized-concept.
Asset type: one Victoria 3 TECHNOLOGY illustration for a historical naval research tree; not a flat production-method pictogram, not a building scene.
Style/medium: restrained hand-painted volumetric game object illustration. Broad painted masses, softened brushed material texture, precise readable silhouette, short restrained highlights and local shadows ON the object. Match the native Victoria 3 navigation chart, mechanical_tools metal hand drill and crystal_glass painted glass objects. Natural material colors; not photoreal, glossy 3D, vector-flat, cartoon sticker, layered cut-paper, steampunk fantasy, or uniformly sepia/blue.
Composition: centered compact group, one dominant object and at most one supporting accessory. Slightly elevated three-quarter view, complete object within a square at least 1024x1024; leave generous fully transparent margins on every side. Strong large shapes for readability at 48 and 64 pixels; fine details subordinate.
Background: genuine alpha transparency outside the objects and through every open gap. All four corners fully transparent. No background color, floor, tabletop, scenic setting, black or grey matte patch, cast-shadow patch, frame, UI tile, disc, decorative medallion or surrounding border.
Text: no readable text, letters, numbers, dates, headings, signatures, logos, labels or watermarks. Short unlettered instrument graduation ticks are allowed; generic chart lines are allowed.
Avoid: extra props, people, hands, flags, coat of arms, glowing outline, neon, beam effects, modern plastic or electrical equipment. Output one finished PNG icon, not a sheet or variants.
Subject: one large silver eighteenth-century marine longitude timekeeper inspired by John Harrison's H4, completed in 1759 (Royal Museums Greenwich ZAA0037). Use its watch-shaped historical silhouette: thick circular silver pair-case, a small winding pendant and open suspension bow at the top, large off-white enamel dial, subtle curved silver rim and short steel hands sharing a central pivot. The timekeeper is seen slightly obliquely so its case thickness is visible, but the dial remains almost frontal and fully legible as a watch. Use simple dark radial tick marks only on the dial, NO Roman numerals, Arabic digits, floral lettering, maker inscriptions or ornament. An understated dark steel central seconds hand may accompany the two thicker hour and minute hands. The dial is warm WHITE, not tan parchment. Silver is neutral-grey with short warm/cool painted glints, not blue chrome; steel hands dark slate. No wooden chronometer box, compass, map, lid covering the dial, stand, chain or extra clockwork; one self-contained scientific watch with substantial material volume, not a flat gold medal or modern wristwatch.

Subject: a compact pale ivory-white nautical survey chart partially unrolled, with curled paper at just one far edge. On it are a simple irregular COASTLINE, small harbour inlet, restrained muted sea-blue wash ONLY inside the chart's sea areas, subtle tan-grey land area, sparse surveying linework and small anonymous depth-mark ticks. No geological colored layers, inland topographic mountain scene, buildings, road or generic text. A single late-eighteenth-century brass sextant lies diagonally across the chart's lower right, based on Jesse Ramsden's circa-1790 sextant (Royal Museums Greenwich NAV1105): broad open triangular metal frame, distinctly CURVED graduated lower arc, straight pivoting index arm, compact horizontal sight telescope, small mirror and dark wooden handle. The sextant is the only accessory and must be large enough that its curved arc and open frame remain recognisable at 48px; simplify small screws and shades. Main chart silhouette about two thirds of the group, sextant about one third, clearly separated in value. Chart ink is lines and tiny anonymous dashes, never letters, sounding numbers or words. Matte nearly-white paper with slight edge wear, patinated warm brass, dark wood, restrained natural palette. Do not add a compass, dividers, quill, ruler or a second instrument; this represents coastal surveying, not ordinary route planning. Transparent gaps inside the sextant where not overlying the chart.

Subject: one early-nineteenth-century Fresnel lighthouse OPTICAL ASSEMBLY, emphasizing the central octagonal drum of stepped glass lenses of the 1823 Cordouan apparatus. This is a simplified conceptual illustration grounded in the Ministry of Culture's historical apparatus reference, not an exact engineering reconstruction or a later 1894 Hourtin model. Show three visible faceted vertical panels in a compact eight-sided metal drum. Each face contains a large circular bull's-eye lens with a few broad CONCENTRIC stepped glass prism rings, strongly legible from the front; side faces angled in perspective. A thin patinated brass/bronze frame joins the panels, with a modest low integral metal foot/base. The glass dominates the object, with restrained clear grey-green/ivory refractive highlights, distinct dark-to-light ring values, and slightly transparent glass, while the metal is muted warm bronze. Broad painted glass bands, not photoreal razor-thin chrome lines or a generic ribbed jar. Keep the silhouette wider and more compact than a tall candle lantern, centered with clear transparent margins. No giant later beehive upper dome, mercury float, modern electrical bulb, lamp cord, lamp flame, beacon glow, extra accessory, whole lighthouse tower, coastal landscape or surrounding protective railing. Distinctive stepped bull's-eye rings convey optical technology; do not turn it into a flat magnifying-glass disc or decorative gold badge.
